h: Aberfoyle treetop tips and Trossachs extras
p: A Go Ape treetop course is a much bigger commitment than a quick climbing session, so plan for a good couple of hours or more on the course itself, plus time for parking, check-in and the safety briefing. It's a decent workout too, so go with a full water bottle and something to eat afterwards.

Once you're up, the instructors stay on the ground and keep an eye on things, which means you need to listen carefully during the briefing. You'll be clipping and unclipping yourself as you move between sections, so the rules matter. Younger participants need an adult with them on the course, and there are set ratios, so check what applies to your group when you book.
Scottish weather can change in minutes, so pack layers, a waterproof and footwear with good grip. The midges can be lively in summer too, so a bit of repellent is no bad idea.

Aberfoyle's surroundings are made for exploring. The Lodge Forest Visitor Centre, right beside the course, is the hub of Queen Elizabeth Forest Park, with trails, waterfalls and wildlife viewing. Loch Ard, just west of the village, is a peaceful spot for a walk by the water. The Lake of Menteith, a few miles east, is home to Inchmahome Priory, a ruined island priory reached by a seasonal ferry. Callander, gateway to the northern Trossachs, is a short drive away for shops and places to eat.
